name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q01 - Hybridisation and physical properties of carbon

questiontext.text:
Consider the following three statements regarding the hybridisation of carbon and its influence on molecular properties:

Statement I: An \(sp\) hybrid orbital contains \(50\%\) \(s\)-character and is held closer to the carbon nucleus than \(sp^2\) and \(sp^3\) hybrid orbitals.

Statement II: As the \(s\)-character of hybrid orbitals increases, the bonds formed by carbon become shorter and have greater bond enthalpies.

Statement III: An increase in the \(s\)-character of carbon hybrid orbitals decreases the electronegativity of the carbon atom.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principles of Orbital Hybridisation
Hybridisation directly determines the spatial distribution, orbital radius, bond length, bond enthalpy, and electronegativity of carbon. The fraction of \(s\)-character in hybrid orbitals follows the sequence: \(sp\) (\(50\%\)) > \(sp^2\) (\(33.3\%\)) > \(sp^3\) (\(25\%\)). Because \(s\) orbitals are spherically symmetric and penetrate closer to the positively charged nucleus than directional \(p\) orbitals, hybrid orbitals with greater \(s\)-character are held tighter and closer to the nucleus.

Step 2: Analysis of Orbital Compactness and Bond Properties
The closer proximity of the \(sp\) hybrid orbital to the nucleus allows for more effective orbital overlap at shorter internuclear distances. Consequently, bonds involving higher \(s\)-character carbons are shorter and stronger (exhibiting higher bond dissociation enthalpies) than those involving lower \(s\)-character carbons (for example, the carbon-carbon triple bond length in ethyne is \(120\text{ pm}\) with a bond enthalpy of \(823\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\), compared to \(154\text{ pm}\) and \(348\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\) for the carbon-carbon single bond in ethane). Therefore, the descriptions of \(s\)-character distribution and resulting bond shortening/strengthening are scientifically valid.

Step 3: Evaluation of Hybridisation Effect on Electronegativity
Because electrons residing in orbitals with greater \(s\)-character experience a stronger effective nuclear attraction, the carbon atom attracts shared electron pairs more strongly towards itself. Thus, the electronegativity of carbon increases directly with increasing \(s\)-character: \(sp\text{-carbon} > sp^2\text{-carbon} > sp^3\text{-carbon}\). The assertion that increasing \(s\)-character decreases the electronegativity of carbon contradicts this fundamental relationship and is factually incorrect.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Only the statements regarding the proximity of the \(sp\) orbital to the nucleus and the resulting increase in bond enthalpy and decrease in bond length are correct, whereas the statement stating a decrease in electronegativity is incorrect. Hence, Statements I and II only are correct.

answer.text: Statements I and II only are correct
Statements II and III only are correct

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q02 - Classification of cyclic and aromatic compounds

questiontext.text:
Consider the following three statements regarding the structural classification of organic compounds:

Statement I: Tetrahydrofuran (THF) is classified as an alicyclic heterocyclic compound.

Statement II: Tropone is an example of a non-benzenoid aromatic compound.

Statement III: Furan, thiophene, and pyridine belong to the class of benzenoid aromatic compounds.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Structural Classification Principles
Organic compounds are systematically classified based on their carbon skeletons into acyclic (open-chain) and cyclic (closed-chain or ring) systems. Cyclic compounds are further divided into homocyclic/carbocyclic (rings composed solely of carbon atoms) and heterocyclic (rings incorporating at least one heteroatom, such as oxygen, nitrogen, or sulphur).

Step 2: Evaluation of Alicyclic Heterocyclic and Non-Benzenoid Ring Systems
Alicyclic compounds contain closed aliphatic rings. Tetrahydrofuran contains a saturated five-membered ring composed of four carbon atoms and one oxygen atom; hence, it is accurately classified as an alicyclic heterocyclic compound. Aromatic compounds are subdivided into benzenoid (containing one or more benzene rings, such as benzene, naphthalene, and aniline) and non-benzenoid (containing aromatic rings devoid of an isolated or fused benzene framework, such as the seven-membered conjugated cyclic ketone tropone). Thus, classifying tropone as a non-benzenoid aromatic compound is chemically accurate.

Step 3: Evaluation of Heterocyclic Aromatic Compounds
Benzenoid aromatic compounds must contain at least one benzene ring structure. Furan (oxygen heteroatom), thiophene (sulphur heteroatom), and pyridine (nitrogen heteroatom) are aromatic systems containing heteroatoms within their conjugated rings. They constitute the distinct class of heterocyclic aromatic compounds, not benzenoid aromatic compounds. Therefore, classifying furan, thiophene, and pyridine as benzenoid aromatic compounds is incorrect.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The characterisation of tetrahydrofuran as an alicyclic heterocycle and tropone as a non-benzenoid aromatic compound is correct, whereas categorising furan, thiophene, and pyridine as benzenoid aromatic compounds is incorrect. Hence, Statements I and II only are correct.

answer.text: Statements I and III only are correct
Statements I and II only are correct

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q03 - Inductive and electromeric electronic displacements

questiontext.text:
Consider the following three statements regarding electronic displacement effects in organic molecules:

Statement I: The inductive effect is a permanent polarization of \(\sigma\)-bonds that decreases rapidly with distance and becomes virtually negligible after three carbon atoms.

Statement II: The electromeric effect is a temporary electron displacement involving the complete transfer of a shared pair of \(\pi\)-electrons to one of the bonded atoms on demand of an attacking reagent.

Statement III: When inductive and electromeric effects operate in opposite directions in an unsaturated molecule, the inductive effect always predominates over the electromeric effect.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Governing Electronic Principles
Electronic displacements in organic molecules are classified as permanent effects (such as the inductive effect, resonance effect, and hyperconjugation) operating in the ground state of the substrate, or temporary effects (such as the electromeric effect and inductomeric effect) operating only during the activation process in the presence of an external attacking reagent.

Step 2: Evaluation of Inductive and Electromeric Effects
The inductive effect arises from differences in electronegativity across \(\sigma\)-bonds, transmitting partial charges along the carbon chain. Because it operates through electrostatic relay via \(\sigma\)-electrons, its magnitude attenuates sharply with distance, becoming negligible beyond three carbon-carbon single bonds. The electromeric effect is specifically defined as the complete transfer of a shared pair of \(\pi\)-electrons to one of the atoms joined by a multiple bond, which occurs strictly when an attacking reagent approaches the substrate and vanishes entirely upon removal of the reagent. Both of these descriptions are fundamentally sound and correct.

Step 3: Hierarchy and Relative Predominance of Opposing Effects
In situations where the permanent inductive effect and the temporary electromeric effect operate in opposite directions during a chemical reaction, the electromeric effect completely predominates. This is because the electromeric effect involves the complete transfer of loosely bound \(\pi\)-electrons under the strong driving force of the approaching electrophile or nucleophile, whereas the inductive effect involves only slight polarization of tightly bound \(\sigma\)-electrons. Thus, stating that the inductive effect predominates over the electromeric effect contradicts established chemical principles.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The definitions and characteristics of the inductive and electromeric effects are scientifically accurate, whereas the stated order of predominance between opposing inductive and electromeric effects is incorrect. Hence, Statements I and II only are correct.

answer.text: Statements I, II and III are all correct
Statements II and III only are correct
Statements I and II only are correct
Statements I and III only are correct

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q04 - Qualitative and quantitative organic analytical methods

questiontext.text:
Consider the following three statements regarding qualitative and quantitative analysis of organic compounds:

Statement I: In Lassaigne's test for nitrogen, the formation of a Prussian blue colouration upon treatment of sodium fusion extract with iron(II) sulphate and dilute sulphuric acid is due to the formation of \(\mathrm{Fe}_4[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_6]_3\cdot x\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\).

Statement II: Kjeldahl's method is not applicable to the quantitative estimation of nitrogen in nitro compounds, azo compounds, and compounds containing nitrogen in a ring (e.g., pyridine), because their nitrogen cannot be converted into ammonium sulphate under standard digestion conditions.

Statement III: Before testing for halogens with silver nitrate solution, the sodium fusion extract is boiled with concentrated nitric acid to decompose any sodium cyanide or sodium sulphide that may interfere by forming insoluble silver salts.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Chemical Reactions in Lassaigne's Nitrogen Detection
Sodium fusion converts covalently bound nitrogen and carbon into ionic sodium cyanide: \(\mathrm{Na} + \mathrm{C} + \mathrm{N} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{NaCN}\). Heating the extract with ferrous sulphate produces sodium hexacyanidoferrate(II):
\[6\mathrm{CN}^- + \mathrm{Fe}^{2+} \rightarrow [\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_6]^{4-}\]
Acidification with concentrated sulphuric acid oxidises some \(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}\) to \(\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}\), which reacts with hexacyanidoferrate(II) to yield a Prussian blue precipitate or solution of iron(III) hexacyanidoferrate(II):
\[4\mathrm{Fe}^{3+} + 3[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_6]^{4-} + x\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \rightarrow \mathrm{Fe}_4[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_6]_3\cdot x\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\]
Thus, this reaction description is fully accurate.

Step 2: Scope and Limitations of Kjeldahl's Method
In Kjeldahl's method, the organic substance is digested with concentrated \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) in the presence of \(\mathrm{CuSO}_4\) and \(\mathrm{K}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) to convert organic nitrogen into \((\mathrm{NH}_4)_2\mathrm{SO}_4\). This method is unsuitable for nitro compounds, azo compounds, and heterocyclic nitrogenous compounds such as pyridine because the nitrogen present in these chemical environments resists reduction and does not get converted to ammonium sulphate under these conditions. Thus, this statement is fully accurate.

Step 3: Elimination of Interfering Ions in Halogen Testing
When both nitrogen or sulphur and halogens are present in the organic compound, the sodium fusion extract contains \(\mathrm{CN}^-\) or \(\mathrm{S}^{2-}\) ions alongside halide ions. Adding silver nitrate directly would precipitate white \(\mathrm{AgCN}\) or black \(\mathrm{Ag}_2\mathrm{S}\), obscuring the identification of silver halides. Boiling the extract with concentrated nitric acid decomposes these interfering species by volatilising them as hydrogen cyanide and hydrogen sulphide:
\[\mathrm{NaCN} + \mathrm{HNO}_3 \rightarrow \mathrm{NaNO}_3 + \mathrm{HCN}\uparrow\]
\[\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{S} + 2\mathrm{HNO}_3 \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NaNO}_3 + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{S}\uparrow\]
Thus, boiling with nitric acid is an essential step to prevent interference.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
All three statements regarding the detection of nitrogen by Prussian blue formation, the scope/limitations of Kjeldahl's method, and the role of nitric acid treatment in halogen testing are chemically valid. Hence, Statements I, II and III are all correct.
